paragraphs: Every eating and drinking that involves a more superior process of extraction (berur) has more blessings instituted for it. Therefore, for eating bread — which is superior in the work of extraction — two blessings were instituted before it: ‘al netilat yadayim’ (on the washing of hands) and ‘hamotzi’, and after it five blessings: the four of Birkat HaMazon and one over the cup. Eating of the seven species, when one eats grain foods (mezonot) or tree fruits of the five species — since this eating is not as superior as eating actual bread — only one blessing was instituted for it afterward, but it is a blessing in the pattern of three (me’ein shalosh) drawn from Birkat HaMazon. And eating fruits of other trees, or produce of the ground, meat, fish, and the like — which is of a lesser level than eating the seven species for which the Land of Israel was praised — no me’ein shalosh blessing was instituted for them, but rather the blessing ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ (Who creates many living things).

Therefore, for the five kinds of fruit that are among the seven species for which the Land of Israel was praised: if one eats a kezayit (olive’s-bulk) of them, which is nine dirhams, one blesses afterward the me’ein shalosh blessing, which is ‘al ha’etz ve’al pri ha’etz’ (for the tree and its fruit), etc., and concludes ‘venodeh lecha Hashem Eloheinu al ha’aretz ve’al haperot, baruch atah Hashem al ha’aretz ve’al haperot’ (we thank You, Lord our God, for the land and for the fruits… blessed are You, Lord, for the land and for the fruits). And these five kinds, if they grew in the Land of Israel itself — whether one eats them in the Land of Israel or outside it — one concludes ‘…al ha’aretz ve’al peroteha, baruch atah Hashem al ha’aretz ve’al peroteha’ (for the land and for its fruits). And if one eats grain foods that grew in the Land of Israel itself, one concludes ‘al ha’aretz ve’al michyah ve’al kalkalatah’ (for the land and for the sustenance and for its provision). The same law applies to wine: after drinking the measure requiring a me’ein shalosh blessing, over wine from outside the Land one concludes ‘venodeh lecha Hashem Eloheinu al ha’aretz ve’al pri hagafen, baruch atah Hashem al ha’aretz ve’al pri hagafen’ (for the land and for the fruit of the vine), and over wine of the Land of Israel one concludes ‘…al ha’aretz ve’al pri gafnah, baruch atah Hashem al ha’aretz ve’al pri gafnah’ (for the land and for the fruit of its vine).

clarification.explanation: The more superior the process of extraction (berur) accomplished through an eating, the more blessings were instituted for it: eating bread (the most superior) — two blessings before it (netilat yadayim, hamotzi) and five after it (the four of Birkat HaMazon plus the blessing over the cup); eating the seven species or grain foods — one blessing at the end (me’ein shalosh); and other fruits/foods — ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ alone. For the five kinds among the seven species, when one eats a kezayit of them — one blesses afterward me’ein shalosh (‘al ha’etz ve’al pri ha’etz’…); if they grew in the Land of Israel — one concludes ‘al ha’aretz ve’al peroteha’; grain foods from the Land of Israel — ‘al ha’aretz ve’al hamichyah ve’al hakalkalah’; wine from outside the Land — ‘al ha’aretz ve’al pri hagafen’; and wine from the Land of Israel — ‘al ha’aretz ve’al pri gafnah.’
takeaways: The final blessing depends on the level of the eating: bread (seven blessings total), the seven species/grain foods (me’ein shalosh), other foods (Borei nefashot rabot).
The wording of me’ein shalosh changes slightly according to the fruit’s origin (Land of Israel or outside it).

paragraphs: The measure of a kezayit for blessing an after-blessing — whether me’ein shalosh or ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ — which is nine dirhams, applies only to eating; but for drinking, whether wine, water, or other beverages, one does not bless an after-blessing until one drinks a revi’it, which is twenty-seven dirhams. However, there are those who disagree and hold that even for beverages the obligation of an after-blessing is at nine dirhams; and although we do not rule so, because of the rule that doubts about blessings are resolved leniently, one who fears Heaven should be careful not to bring himself into this doubt — rather, he should either drink less than nine dirhams and not bless according to any opinion, or drink twenty-seven dirhams and bless according to all opinions.

clarification.explanation: The measure of a kezayit for an after-blessing (me’ein shalosh or Borei nefashot rabot) is nine dirhams — this applies to eating only; for drinking — one does not bless an after-blessing except after a revi’it, which is twenty-seven dirhams. There are those who disagree and hold that for beverages too, the measure of a kezayit (nine dirhams) suffices, but the halachah is not so; one who fears Heaven should be careful not to enter this doubt — he should drink less than nine dirhams (and then not bless according to any opinion), or drink twenty-seven dirhams (and then bless according to all opinions).
takeaways: An after-blessing on eating applies from the measure of a kezayit (nine dirhams); on drinking — only from the measure of a revi’it (twenty-seven dirhams).

paragraphs: In the me’ein shalosh blessing — whether of grain foods, of wine, or of the five species of the Land of Israel — one must mention the special occasion (mei’ein hama’oreh) on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh; and if one forgot, one is not required to go back. And if one already said ‘ki atah tov u’metiv lakol’ without having mentioned the special occasion, one should not mention it anymore — just as we hold regarding Birkat HaMazon, that if one has begun the fourth blessing, one can no longer mention the special occasion, so too is the law here — because ‘ki atah tov u’metiv’ is like a fourth blessing. For even though this blessing is called ‘me’ein shalosh’ (in the pattern of three), it is in truth ‘me’ein arba’ (in the pattern of four), and it is called ‘me’ein shalosh’ because the first three are from the Torah, and therefore it is named after them — so is the opinion of the Eliyah Rabbah, Siman 208, se’if katan 20. However, the annotator in Chesed LaAlafim, Siman 208, chiddush 4, challenged this and wrote that a distinction should be made — see there. And therefore I have concluded in my holy book Makabtziel: since one has already said ‘ki atah tov u’metiv lakol,’ one should not mention the special occasion explicitly, but should reflect on the matter in his heart and then conclude the blessing.

clarification.explanation: In the blessing me’ein shalosh — whether of grain foods, of wine, or of the five kinds of fruit of the Land of Israel — one must mention the special occasion on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh; and if one forgot, one does not go back. And if one has already said ‘ki atah tov u’metiv lakol’ without having mentioned the special occasion — one should not mention it anymore, just as in Birkat HaMazon, if one has begun the fourth blessing, one can no longer mention the special occasion. The reason: ‘ki atah tov u’metiv’ is like a fourth blessing — for even though this blessing is called me’ein shalosh, it is in truth me’ein arba, and is named after the three because they are from the Torah (per the Eliyah Rabbah); however, the annotator in Chesed LaAlafim challenged this and made a distinction. Therefore the Ben Ish Chai concluded (in Makabtziel): if one has already said ‘ki atah tov u’metiv lakol’ — one should not mention the special occasion explicitly, but should reflect on the matter in his heart and then conclude the blessing.
takeaways: Me’ein shalosh — one mentions the special occasion on Shabbat/Yom Tov/Rosh Chodesh; if one forgot — one does not go back.
If one has already said ‘ki atah tov u’metiv lakol’ (which is like a fourth blessing) — one should not mention it explicitly, but reflect on it in one’s heart and conclude.

paragraphs: One who ate fruits of the seven species, and also grain foods, and also drank wine, should include all three together in one after-blessing, giving precedence to ‘hamichyah,’ then ‘hagafen,’ then ‘ha’etz.’

clarification.explanation: One who ate fruits of the seven species, and also grain foods, and also drank wine — includes all three in one blessing (me’ein shalosh), giving precedence to ‘hamichyah,’ then ‘hagafen,’ then ‘ha’etz.’
takeaways: One who ate grain foods, wine, and fruits of the seven species — blesses one blessing including all of them, in the order: grain foods, wine, tree fruit.

paragraphs: All foods combine to reach the measure of a kezayit, but eating and drinking do not combine with each other; however, bread soaked in a beverage — the beverage absorbed within it combines toward the measure of a kezayit. And what we say, that all foods combine to a kezayit, applies specifically to blessing ‘Borei nefashot rabot’; but for the me’ein shalosh blessing, if one ate half a kezayit of the five species and half a kezayit of other fruits, one should not bless me’ein shalosh, but rather bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ — see Tov Ayin by the Gaon Chida, page 44. The same law applies if one ate half a kezayit of the five species and half a kezayit of grain foods or half a kezayit of bread — they do not combine, and one blesses ‘Borei nefashot rabot.’ But the five kinds of fruit of the seven species combine with each other: if one ate half a kezayit of grapes and half a kezayit of figs, or pomegranates, or olives, or dates, they combine with each other to bless me’ein shalosh; and if one ate half a kezayit of grain food and half a kezayit of bread, one blesses me’ein shalosh.

clarification.explanation: Different foods combine together to reach the measure of a kezayit (for the purpose of ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ only), but eating and drinking do not combine with each other (except for bread soaked in a beverage, where the absorbed beverage combines). Regarding the me’ein shalosh blessing: fruits of the seven species combine with each other (for example, half a kezayit of grapes and half a kezayit of figs), but they do not combine with fruits/grain foods that are not of the seven species; half a kezayit of grain food and half a kezayit of bread do combine for me’ein shalosh.
takeaways: Grain foods and different eatings combine for ‘Borei nefashot rabot’; for me’ein shalosh — only within matching groups (the seven species among themselves, or grain foods with bread).

paragraphs: If one ate fruits whose blessing is me’ein shalosh, and also ate fruits whose blessing is ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ — even though one ate a measure of a kezayit of each — one need not bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot,’ for these are exempted by the me’ein shalosh blessing that he now blesses.

clarification.explanation: One who ate both fruits whose blessing is me’ein shalosh and fruits whose blessing is ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ (a kezayit measure of each) — need not bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ separately, because they are exempted by the me’ein shalosh blessing that he blesses.
takeaways: The me’ein shalosh blessing also exempts other foods whose blessing is ‘Borei nefashot rabot,’ if eaten together.

paragraphs: If one ate half a kezayit, paused, and then ate another half a kezayit — if the time from the beginning of the first half-kezayit to the end of the last half-kezayit does not exceed the measure of ‘achilat peras’ (the measure of three eggs, which is fifty-four dirhams), these two eatings combine and one blesses the after-blessing; and if not, they do not combine and one does not bless. And although there are those who disagree and hold that in optional (non-obligatory) eating, if one ate the full measure, even if one paused for the duration of achilat peras, one blesses the after-blessing — for this law was stated only regarding an obligatory eating, such as matzah on the night of Pesach or a kezayit of bread on the first night of Sukkot in the sukkah — nevertheless, since we hold that doubts about blessings are resolved leniently, [the stricter view is followed] — see Zechor LeAvraham, part 3, in the final treatise, and other latter authorities not mentioned there. However, it appears to me that one should bless without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty, and reflect on the name and sovereignty in his heart. And if this happens to him and he is able to complete the measure without pausing and then bless, a blessing will come upon him. All this is regarding eating; but regarding drinking, if one drank a little, paused, and then completed the measure — it combines only if the total time from beginning to end fits within the measure of drinking a revi’it; otherwise they do not combine.

clarification.explanation: One who ate half a kezayit, paused, and then ate another half a kezayit — if the total elapsed time (from the beginning of the first eating to the end of the second) is less than the measure of ‘achilat peras’ (about the size of three eggs, roughly 54 dirhams) — the two eatings combine for the after-blessing; if more — they do not combine, and one does not bless (or blesses without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty, reflecting on the name and sovereignty in his heart); and if he is able to complete the measure without pausing and then bless, it is praiseworthy to do so. There are those who disagree and hold that this law (that a long pause invalidates the combination) was stated only regarding an obligatory eating, such as matzah on the night of Pesach or a kezayit of bread on the first night of Sukkot — but for an optional eating, even if one paused for the duration of achilat peras, the eatings combine and one blesses the after-blessing; but despite this dispute, in practice the stricter opinion is followed, because doubts about blessings are resolved leniently. In drinking — it combines only if the entire drinking took place within the measure of drinking a revi’it.
takeaways: Too long a pause (more than ‘achilat peras’) between two eatings of the same food invalidates the combination for the after-blessing.

Some hold that for optional eating (unlike obligatory eating such as matzah on the night of Pesach), the pause does not invalidate the combination, but in practice the stricter view is followed out of doubt about blessings.

paragraphs: One who sucks the juice of fruits is considered to be eating, with the measure of a kezayit — but this is specifically when he sucks them by chewing, placing them in his mouth, since he must chew with his teeth, he is treated as one who eats, with the measures of a kezayit. But sucking that does not involve chewing, such as one who sucks an orange (portokal) or a small citrus fruit (naranj — a sour citrus), and the like, holding the fruit in his hand and sucking it — since there is no chewing involved, this is treated as drinking; and even if he sucked the measure of a revi’it, he does not bless an after-blessing, because for drinking we require that one not pause from the beginning to the end of the measure of drinking a revi’it, and one who sucks cannot suck the measure of a revi’it without pausing more than the time of drinking a revi’it. Therefore, any fruit that one does not suck by way of chewing — one does not bless an after-blessing even if one sucks a great deal — see Kol Eliyahu, Siman 7, there.

clarification.explanation: Sucking the juice of a fruit is considered eating (with the measure of a kezayit) only if it involves chewing (placing it in the mouth and chewing). But sucking without chewing (such as sucking an orange by hand without placing it in the mouth to chew) is treated as drinking — therefore even if one sucked the measure of a revi’it, one does not bless an after-blessing, because it is impossible to suck in this way without pausing for too long.
takeaways: Sucking a fruit with chewing — is treated as eating (kezayit); sucking without chewing — is treated as drinking, and does not reach an after-blessing (because it takes too long).

paragraphs: One should not bless an after-blessing over a hot beverage, such as coffee (qahwa) or tea (chai) and the like, because one cannot drink from them the measure of a revi’it without pausing, that is, within the measure of drinking a revi’it, due to their being hot. The same law applies to one who drinks cold water in the winter days, who is forced to drink little by little because of the coldness, and pauses at length during his drinking.

clarification.explanation: One does not bless an after-blessing over a hot beverage (coffee, tea), because it is impossible to drink the measure of a revi’it from it in one continuous span (due to the heat, one drinks it slowly, little by little). The same applies to very cold water in winter that causes one to drink slowly.
takeaways: A hot beverage (or one too cold) that causes slow drinking — has no after-blessing on it, because one cannot drink a revi’it in one continuous span.

paragraphs: If one did not intend to eat more than half the measure, because he wanted to eat only one apple, which is half the measure, and it was brought to him and he ate it, and afterward he desired another apple, and it was brought to him and he blessed over it and ate it — even though the time from the beginning of eating the first apple to the end of eating the second apple did not exceed the measure of achilat peras, nevertheless the halachic authorities were uncertain whether these two eatings combine for the after-blessing, and the matter remains in doubt regarding blessings. Therefore, one should not bring himself into this matter, unless he eats a full measure the second time; and if he transgressed and ate without doing so and has no more to complete the measure, he should bless without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty, and reflect on the name and sovereignty in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who intended to eat only half a measure (one apple), and afterward changed his mind and ate an additional apple (with a separate blessing) — there is doubt as to whether the two eatings combine for the after-blessing, even if they were in sequence (within the measure of achilat peras). Therefore he should not bring himself into this doubt, but should eat a full measure the second time, or bless without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty if this has already occurred.
takeaways: Eating that was not originally planned as a whole (half-and-half with separate intentions) — is in doubt regarding the after-blessing; it is preferable to complete a full measure.

paragraphs: One who drank wine and also other beverages does not bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ over the beverages, since the blessing ‘al hagefen’ exempts them. And if he drank water or other beverages before drinking the wine, there are those who say that ‘al hagefen’ does not exempt them retroactively, and there are those who say that it exempts them even in this case. Therefore one must be careful not to bring himself into a doubt about blessings, and should bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ over the water or other beverages before drinking the wine; and if he did not do so, he should bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty, because of the rule that doubts about blessings are resolved leniently.

clarification.explanation: One who drank wine and also other beverages — does not bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ on the beverages, because the blessing of ‘hagefen’ exempts them. But if he drank other beverages (water and the like) before drinking the wine, there is a dispute: some say that the blessing of hagefen does not exempt them retroactively, and some say that it exempts them even in this case too. Therefore one must be careful not to enter a doubt about blessings, and should bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ over the water or other beverages before drinking the wine. And if he was not careful about this, he should bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty, because of the doubt.
takeaways: After wine, one does not bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ on other beverages — the blessing of hagefen exempts them.
If one drinks another beverage before the wine, it is preferable to bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ on it immediately, before drinking the wine, so as not to enter a doubt.
If one was not careful and already drank a beverage before the wine, one should bless ‘Borei nefashot rabot’ without mentioning God’s name and sovereignty.

paragraphs: If one ate or drank the requisite measure and immediately vomited it, he does not bless an after-blessing — see the latter authorities.

clarification.explanation: One who ate or drank the requisite measure and immediately vomited it — does not bless an after-blessing.
takeaways: Immediate vomiting after eating/drinking exempts one from the after-blessing.

paragraphs: One should be careful to bless the me’ein shalosh blessing while seated, since there are those who say that it is an obligation from the Torah; and one who is stringent to bless me’ein shalosh with closed eyes, like Birkat HaMazon, a blessing will come upon him.

clarification.explanation: The me’ein shalosh blessing should be blessed while seated (there are those who hold that it is from the Torah), and one who is stringent to bless it with closed eyes, like Birkat HaMazon — a blessing will come upon him.
takeaways: Me’ein shalosh — is blessed while seated (and preferably also with closed eyes).

paragraphs: A person does not answer ‘Amen’ after his own blessings, unless he said two blessings or more, in which case he says ‘Amen’ at the end of the blessings; therefore, one who blesses the blessings of the Haftarah answers ‘Amen’ after the blessings of the Haftarah. And a listener among Israel blesses along with one of all the blessings, even if he did not hear it entirely from the start, and is obligated to answer ‘Amen’ to it; and the one answering should also have in mind to include the one blessing, so as to fulfill for him his obligation of answering ‘Amen’; and therefore one must answer in a voice loud enough for the one blessing to hear, and the one blessing must also intend to fulfill the listener’s obligation. But the one answering should be careful not to raise his voice louder than the one blessing. And the holy Zohar was very stringent regarding the punishment of one who hears a blessing and does not answer ‘Amen.’ Therefore, if one who blesses over something for himself sees that the listeners treat the matter with contempt and do not answer, it is better that he bless quietly so that they will not hear the blessing and come to stumble — as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, Siman 215, letter 3.

clarification.explanation: One does not answer ‘Amen’ after one’s own blessings, unless one said two or more blessings in sequence — in which case one answers ‘Amen’ at the end of all of them (such as one who blesses the blessings of the Haftarah). One who hears a blessing from a fellow Jew — even if he did not hear it all from the beginning — is obligated to answer ‘Amen’ (aloud, so that the one blessing can hear, and with intent to fulfill the listener’s obligation) — but not louder than the one blessing. If the listeners treat the matter with contempt and do not answer ‘Amen,’ it is better to bless quietly so that they will not come to stumble.
takeaways: One answers ‘Amen’ to one’s own blessing only if one said two consecutive blessings; answering ‘Amen’ to another’s blessing is obligatory even without hearing all of it.

paragraphs: When one hears another praying for something, or blessing on behalf of Israel, even without mention of God’s name, he is obligated to answer ‘Amen’; therefore one must answer ‘Amen’ after ‘HaRachaman’ in Birkat HaMazon, and likewise one must answer ‘Amen’ when the prayer leader recites ‘Mi shebeirach’ for the congregation, and likewise they shall answer ‘Amen’ when the prayer leader says, before Musaf on Shemini Atzeret and on the first day of Pesach: ‘Begishmei orah ta’ir adamah, etc.’ [with rain], ‘Betiklei orah ta’ir adamah, etc.’ [with dew]; and likewise in the Selichot, when he says ‘Eloheinu shebashamayim, etc.,’ the congregation shall answer ‘Amen’ — and so on for all similar cases.

clarification.explanation: One who hears a person praying or blessing on behalf of Israel (even without mention of God’s name) is obligated to answer ‘Amen’; therefore one answers ‘Amen’ after ‘HaRachaman’ in Birkat HaMazon, after the ‘Mi shebeirach’ of the prayer leader, and in the wording of the Selichot that contain similar requests.
takeaways: One answers ‘Amen’ also on requests/blessings for the congregation that do not mention God’s name (HaRachaman, Mi shebeirach, Selichot).

paragraphs: One should teach his young children to answer ‘Amen,’ for as soon as a child answers ‘Amen,’ he has a share in the World to Come; and a person is obligated to answer ‘Amen’ after children who bless — but only if they are blessing in earnest; if they are merely reciting the text of the blessings as a form of learning, in order to practice, one does not answer ‘Amen’ after them. And anyone who blesses an unnecessary blessing — it is forbidden to answer ‘Amen’ after him. And anyone who alters the formula that our Sages instituted for blessings, in a way that invalidates it, one does not answer ‘Amen’ after him — and all the more so if he omitted God’s name and sovereignty from a blessing in which they were instituted; indeed, even if he omitted only the word ‘ha’olam’ [the world], one does not answer ‘Amen’ after him.

clarification.explanation: One should teach young children to answer ‘Amen’ — the very act of a child answering ‘Amen’ earns him a share in the World to Come, and one is obligated to answer after their blessing. But if they are merely reciting the wording of the blessings (without genuine intent to bless), as a form of learning — one does not answer after them. One does not answer ‘Amen’ after an unnecessary blessing, or a blessing whose formula was altered in an invalidating way, and all the more so if one omitted God’s name and sovereignty (or even just the word ‘ha’olam’).
takeaways: Children are taught to answer ‘Amen’ (it earns them merit); one does not answer to a blessing recited merely for practice, an unnecessary blessing, or a corrupted blessing (especially missing God’s name and sovereignty).
